# Distributions {.hero #s04-distributions}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="4"}
Seminar 4 · Binomial, Poisson, exponential, normal
:::

Four names for one story.

::: {.lede}
The worksheet presents these as four separate recipes with four separate tables. They are not separate. Three of them are the *same stream of events* asked different questions, and the fourth shows up whenever you add things together.
:::

## Where the binomial comes from {.stage-slide #binom-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="binom-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="binom-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="binom-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="binom-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The count discards *which* trials succeeded, so all 120 orderings of three successes collapse into one bar — C(n,k) is exactly how many collapsed.
:::

## Which seller do you trust? {.stage-slide #seller-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="seller-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="seller-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="seller-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="seller-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Same formula as the last slide, turned around: there we fixed the rate and asked which counts were likely; here we fix the count we saw and ask which rates are. More reviews narrow the curve — but narrow is not the same as good, and the 93% seller is merely *precisely* mediocre. Below $s=0.5$ every curve is flat against zero, which is why the axis starts there.
:::

## Ten out of ten is weak evidence {.sim-slide #seller-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · likelihood, and a decision
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-plot}
```{webr-r}
#| fig-width: 5.7
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
s <- seq(0.5, 1, length.out = 401)
L   <- function(k, n) dbinom(k, n, s)
rel <- function(k, n) L(k, n) / max(L(k, n))
plot(s, rel(10, 10), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     col = "#325D88", xlab = "true rate s",
     ylab = "relative likelihood", las = 1)
lines(s, rel(48, 50), lwd = 2, col = "#93C54B")
lines(s, rel(186, 200), lwd=2, col="#B94A48")
# flat prior: s ~ Beta(k + 1, n - k + 1)
good <- function(k,n) 1 - pbeta(.95, k+1, n-k+1)
round(c(A = good(10, 10), B = good(48, 50),
        C = good(186, 200)), 4)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
10/10 gives only a **0.43** chance the true rate beats 95%; 48/50 gives **0.47** and wins. Try `good(100, 100)`: **it was never the percentage, but how much rested on it.**
:::

## Hold $np$ fixed and push $n$ up {.stage-slide #pois-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="pois-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="pois-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="pois-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="pois-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Watch what is lost: at $n = 1000$ you can no longer recover $n$ or $p$ from the shape — only their product. That is why the Poisson has *one* parameter, and why it suits events with no natural "number of trials" at all.
:::

## The same events, a different question {.stage-slide #expo-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="expo-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="expo-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="expo-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="expo-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
One timeline, two distributions. Count per interval and you get Poisson; measure the gaps and you get exponential. The last step is the exponential's defining property — the re-normalised remaining waits land back on the *same* curve.
:::

## Memorylessness is not a figure of speech {.sim-slide #memory-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · the exponential's defining property
:::

::: {.lede-min}
A machine has lasted 10 years. Is it now more likely to fail soon? If lifetimes are exponential, the answer is exactly no — and that is a strong, testable claim.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
x <- rexp(500000, rate = 0.1)  # mean life 10y
s <- 10                        # <-- survived

fresh <- mean(x > 5)
used  <- mean(x > s + 5) / mean(x > s)

round(c(new_5_more  = fresh,
        used_5_more = used), 4)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Both land on 0.607. A brand-new machine and a 10-year-old one have the *same* chance of surviving another five years. Change `s` to anything you like — it never matters. **This is also why the exponential is often the wrong model for physical wear.**
:::

## Why the normal turns up at all {.stage-slide #clt-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="clt-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="clt-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="clt-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="clt-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The population on the left never changes and never becomes normal. It is the **mean** that does — and it also narrows, at the rate $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Both panels share one axis so the narrowing is real, not an artefact of rescaling.
:::

## One table for every normal {.stage-slide #zstd-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="zstd-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="zstd-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="zstd-frag-2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Subtracting $\mu$ moves the curve; dividing by $\sigma$ squeezes it — and a squeezed density must grow *taller*, because the area underneath is always 1. The shaded probability never moves. Standardising changes the ruler, not the answer.
:::

## Check the approximation {.sim-slide #pois-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · exact vs approximate
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Three mistakes per 10,000 transactions; 10,000 audited. What is the chance of four or more? Compute it both ways.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
n <- 10000; p <- 0.0003   # <-- keep n * p = 3
mu <- n * p

# P(4 or more mistakes)
exact  <- 1 - pbinom(3, n, p)
approx <- 1 - ppois(3, mu)

round(c(binomial = exact,
        poisson  = approx,
        gap      = exact - approx), 6)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The gap rounds to zero at six decimal places — the approximation costs you nothing here. Now set `n <- 20; p <- 0.15` (still $np = 3$) and watch it open up. **That** is what "large $n$, small $p$" is protecting you from.
:::

## Break the bell on purpose {.sim-slide #clt-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 4 · the CLT, stress-tested
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-plot}
```{webr-r}
#| fig-width: 5.7
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
n <- 5          # <-- draws per average
reps <- 4000
# a population with no bell shape at all
pop <- function(k) rexp(k, rate = 1)^2
sigma <- sd(pop(200000))
xbar <- replicate(reps, mean(pop(n)))
hist(xbar, breaks = 40, col = "#CBD9E6",
     border = "white", las = 1, main = "",
     xlab = paste("mean of", n, "draws"))
round(c(sd_obs  = sd(xbar),
        se_pred = sigma/sqrt(n)), 3)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
`n <- 1` is the raw population, violently skewed; by `n <- 30` it is nearly symmetric and `sd_obs` tracks $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. **The CLT is a claim about the mean, and it survives a parent this ugly.**
:::
